html:
Song of Lawino is a long poem by the Ugandan poet Okot p'Bitek, first written in the Acholi language and published in his own English version in 1966. It became one of the best-loved works of East African literature.

The speaker is Lawino, an Acholi woman whose husband Ocol has gone to university and now scorns her and everything Acholi. He prefers a westernised woman, ballroom dancing, the clock and the Bible, and calls his own people's ways primitive. Lawino answers him in a long, funny and bitter complaint, defending Acholi dance, cooking, medicine and beauty, and mocking the new elite who copy Europe without thinking.

The poem borrows the forms of Acholi song and voice, and it caught the mood of Uganda just after independence. Okot followed it with Song of Ocol (1970), the husband's reply. Song of Lawino opened a style of "song" poetry in East Africa and fed the debate that Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o later framed as decolonising the mind.
